--- title: "From ggplot2, in five edits" description: "The same penguin plot written in ggplot2 and in vellumplot, five mechanical edits apart. Then one more line makes it a live widget, and two more make it an animation." categories: [Basics, Interactive, Animation] image: figs/from-ggplot2-vellum.png --- If you write ggplot2, you can already read vellumplot. The grammar is the same: data, marks mapped to columns, scales, labels, a theme. What changes is the spelling, and the change is mechanical. Here is one plot of the Palmer Penguins written both ways. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pen <- palmerpenguins::penguins pen <- pen[complete.cases(pen), ] pal <- c(Adelie = "#c0603a", Chinstrap = "#7a5195", Gentoo = "#3d7a6b") ``` ::: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="49%"} **ggplot2** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gg <- ggplot(pen, aes(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, colour = species)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.7) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) + scale_colour_manual(values = pal) + labs(title = "Bigger flippers, heavier penguins", x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", colour = "Species") + theme_minimal() ggsave("penguins.png", gg, width = 6, height = 4) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="2%"} ::: ::: {.column width="49%"} **vellumplot** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} vp <- vplot(pen, width = 6, height = 4) |> mark_point(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species, alpha = 0.7) |> mark_smooth(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species, method = "lm", se = FALSE) |> scale_colour_manual(values = pal) |> labs(title = "Bigger flippers, heavier penguins", x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", colour = "Species") |> theme_minimal() render_plot(vp, "penguins.png") ``` ::: ::: :::: ## The five edits 1. **`ggplot(data, aes(...))` becomes `vplot(data)`.** The call takes the data and nothing else. There is no plot-wide `aes()`. 2. **`+` becomes `|>`.** Each step is an ordinary function that takes a plot and returns a plot, so the native pipe chains them. 3. **`aes()` becomes named arguments on the mark.** `x = flipper_length_mm` goes straight into `mark_point()`, and because nothing is inherited, every layer names its own columns. A constant, like `alpha = 0.7`, sits next to the mappings: a column name maps, a value sets. 4. **`geom_*()` becomes `mark_*()`.** `geom_point()` is `mark_point()`, `geom_smooth()` is `mark_smooth()`, and the arguments mean what they meant. 5. **The size moves into the plot.** ggplot2 learns the page size when you save; vellumplot is told up front, in `vplot(width = , height = )`, because it lays the figure out before drawing it. `render_plot()` then writes the file. What stays: `scale_colour_manual()`, `labs()` and `theme_minimal()` keep their names and arguments, and so does the British spelling. `colour` and `color` are both accepted. ## The two pictures ::: {layout-ncol=2} ![ggplot2](figs/from-ggplot2-gg.png){fig-alt="Scatter plot of penguin flipper length against body mass, coloured by species with a straight fit per species, drawn by ggplot2"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![vellumplot](figs/from-ggplot2-vellum.png){fig-alt='The same scatter plot drawn by vellumplot: penguin flipper length against body mass, coloured by species with a fitted line per species' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: They are not pixel copies. The two packages pick slightly different point sizes, line widths and legend keys, and the fonts come from different text engines. But it is the same plot: same data, same fits, same scales, same theme. ## One more line: a widget The spec above has never been drawn by a graphics device. It is a description of the plot, and anything that can read it can host it. Pipe it into `as_widget()` and the same figure becomes interactive in the browser: hover a point, click a species in the legend, drag to brush, scroll to zoom. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} vp |> as_widget() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: There is no second plotting engine behind that. The widget ships the SVG that vellum solved plus a table of where every mark landed, so it cannot disagree with the PNG above. ## Two more lines: an animation Penguins were measured in three seasons, 2007 to 2009. `transition_states(year)` turns the plot into one keyframe per season and `animate()` tweens between them. The scales are trained once over all three years and frozen, so the axes and the colours never move; only the birds and the fitted lines do. One argument is new. Each season is a different set of penguins, so the points get a `data_id`: with it, the tween fades one season's birds out and the next season's in, instead of sliding a 2007 penguin onto a 2008 one. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pen$id <- seq_len(nrow(pen)) a <- vplot(pen, width = 6, height = 4) |> mark_point(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species, alpha = 0.7, data_id = id) |> mark_smooth(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species, method = "lm", se = FALSE) |> scale_colour_manual(values = pal) |> labs(title = "Penguins measured in {closest_state}", x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", colour = "Species") |> theme_minimal() |> transition_states(year) |> animate(nframes = 60, fps = 20) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](figs/from-ggplot2-anim.png){fig-alt='Animation cycling through the 2007, 2008 and 2009 penguin seasons: points fade between seasons while the per-species fitted lines shift slightly' width=100%} ::: ::: The title is a template: `{closest_state}` is filled in on every frame. For more, see the [animation pages](index.qmd#category=Animation) and the [widget pages](index.qmd#category=Interactive).
